La oferta de dinero real $M/P$ iguala a: The real money supply $M/P$ equals money demand, $L = k · Y − h · i$: more money is demanded when income is higher (to pay for transactions) and less when the rate, which is the cost of holding it instead of bonds, is high. The LM curve slopes upward.

Un aumento del gasto autónomo $A$ despla: An increase in autonomous spending $A$ shifts the IS curve to the right, but income rises less than with the Keynesian multiplier $1/(1 − c_1)$: more income raises the rate and the rate holds back investment (crowding out). An increase in the real money supply shifts the LM curve down, lowers the rate and stimulates investment and income. If investment does not react to the rate (small b) fiscal policy is very effective; if money demand is very sensitive to the rate (huge h, liquidity trap) the LM curve is almost flat: fiscal policy works with its full multiplier and monetary policy does almost nothing.
